#4454. New Zealand’s Twin-Engine Toyota Celica Is Essentially Unstoppable

A fairly conventional overlanding Celica build quickly spiraled into a monster with two engines, dual gearboxes, and semi-amphibious capability.

The art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free. Sure, there are never-ending hoops to jump through for street legality, but actually building your perfect vehicle is merely a matter of dreams. For Kiwi Gareth Wadsworth, who goes by @garethcars on social media, those dreams meant stuffing two engines and two transmissions into a single sixth-generation Toyota Celica. Seems easy enough, right?

Wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos. The basic recipe is a pair of Toyota’s 2.0-liter 3S-GE engines—one mounted in the front and one mounted in the rear—mated to a pair of manual transmissions and fed to individual differentials.

With so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine. If you press directly in the middle of the accelerator, both engines will rev up (somewhat) in sync. Wadsworth emphasized that it is two completely separate drivetrains that require two of everything (two batteries, two fuel tanks, two ECUs, two radiators) and can be driven separately or simultaneously.

But this Celica build wasn’t always this extreme. In fact, the initial version was supposed to be a simple overlanding setup for a university off-road club trip in 2020. He initially off-roaded the Celica with a simple four-inch lift kit and 31-inch tires, but Wadsworth wanted to try something more extreme—and he didn’t want to abandon the existing platform.

“I had this Celica that I bought crashed, and I didn't have anything to do with it. I was a student. I didn't have the money for a four-wheel-drive, so I ended up building it into a four-wheel-drive,” Wadsworth said to Road & Track. “I paid $800 for the car, and then I sold the wheels and tires that were on it. So it was effectively a free car just sitting around, and I got some suspension left over from other projects that I threw in it, and the engine came from a crashed car I found upside down off the side of the road.”

After a year of mud-slinging fun, Wadsworth decided to go all-in on the dual-engine swap. The rear engine transplant only took two weeks, with most of the work happening after school and during a series of all-nighters. A day or two after the build was complete, Wadsworth and friends trailered the dual-engine Celica to an off-road area and began testing its abilities. Some limitations were quickly revealed.

“It was just the stock intakes for a few trips. It did have a snorkel on the outside for the front engine. Once it was twin-engine, it had enough power that we could hit the water faster, and that meant that the bow wave would keep going over the roof and filling the front engine's snorkel. We had one trip on the White Bear River that was in flood, and we hydrolocked the front engine twenty-three times, and we got sick of having to pull the spark plugs out, blasting the water out, and trying to get it running again. And so that's why I moved the intake to the glove box,” Wadsworth said.

Wading is one of the twin-engine Celica’s best tricks, as it is fast enough to glide onto the water and light enough to float through. The Celica has floated through currents that have sunk heavier 4x4 trucks, Wadsworth said. But the twin-engine Celica doesn’t just excel at water crossings, either. Because the gearboxes run independently, Wadsworth can tune the gear ratios of either end to suit his needs.

“There's no weird handling from the differences between the front and rear. It's just whichever engine's got the least load on it speeds up to catch up with the other one. They're effectively a fifty-fifty split,” Wadsworth said. “Because of the biasing, I quite often run almost exclusively rear-wheel-drive, and I only add front when I need it for traction. It's quite a unique feeling. It's so much fun, and probably the main reason I've still got it is being able to dynamically shift between front, rear, or four-wheel-drive and throttle biasing on the fly. In a mud pit, I can sit around doing donuts with the front in neutral, and then I can put the front-end gear in and let the clutch out slowly on the front to transition from donuts to power slides.”

And it isn’t even too hard to drive—relatively speaking. Wadsworth said that his mates can hop in and romp it with minimal coaching, at least in this configuration. Shifting the two gearboxes can get awkward, but the rear transmission shifter is placed near the traditional shifter, so you don’t have to reach far. Before the pulley clutch system, Wadsworth wired the rear clutch through the parking brake, which required a gentle touch to keep from stalling.

But it wasn’t always so accommodating. “On the original build, we didn't have time to connect any of the controls, so it had two drivers back then. And we didn't have a throttle, so the strap for tightening the hood was tied onto the rearview mirror and back to the rear throttle body, and you pulled it like a train horn,” Wadsworth said. “We certainly had a lot of difficulty driving it when we first built it, because it required two people to communicate—but it didn't have any exhaust, so we couldn't hear each other, and we had no total control on the rear; it was either fully on or fully off. And you had to get up out of your seat, turn around, and put it in gear for the rear engine.”

Even after six years of ownership and five years with two engines, Wadsworth plans to continue driving the twin-engine Celica as long as possible. Initially, he considered adding four-wheel steering using a power steering motor from a Nissan Leaf, but he said the time under the knife wouldn’t be worth it. The more time spent off-road, the better.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4452. Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport is the electric hot hatch we want, but can’t have

Volkswagen revealed the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, an electric pocket rocket with a massive rear wing and 362 horsepower.

We knew Volkswagen was cooking something “really spicy” up after teasing the new GTI hot hatch earlier this week.

Volkswagen launched the first-generation Golf GTI in 1976, which essentially defined the hot hatch. To celebrate the brand’s legendary performance badge, a signature of its sporty, practical hatchbacks, VW is entering a new era with its first fully electric GTI.

The GTI has been “one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years,” Volkswagen’s technical development boss, Kai Grünitz, said.

After opening pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, the brand’s first EV to wear the badge, Volkswagen introduced the Clubsport Concept, a souped-up two-door electric pocket rocket.

The new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept shows “how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world,” according to Grünitz.

It’s based on the production ID. Polo GTI uses the same MEB+ platform, but VW reengineered it with a larger electric motor to pump out more power.

The Clubsport is powered by a 362 hp (270 kW) front-mounted electric motor (APP550) that’s typically used in the rear of VW’s larger EVs, like the ID. Tiguan and the ID.7. That’s up considerably from the 233 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft of torque of the standard ID. Polo GTI offers.

Thomas Schmall, CEO of Volkswagen Group Components, said the APP550 motor is “one of the most efficient electric drives in its class.”

Thanks to an electronically controlled front differential lock (VAQ), Volkswagen said, the Clubsport version can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 4.7 seconds, beating the standard ID. Polo GTI by a full two seconds (6.8 seconds).

Volkswagen also fine-tuned the adaptive chassis control (DCC) to make it racetrack-ready and added new ceramic brakes to help slow it down.

The Clubsport version uses the same 52 kW NMC battery as the ID. Polo GTI, which can provide up to 389 hp (290 kW), Volkswagen said, enabling a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h).

On the exterior, the Clubsport is a two-door model rather than a four-door. It’s 100 mm longer than the standard ID. Polo GTI, with each wing flared an additional 50 mm. It also gets a large motorsport splitter up front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser, and a massive carbon-fiber rear wing.

Inside, the cabin is tailored to the racetrack with a minimalist, stripped-down, two-seater layout. As such, there’s no infotainment system, just a center display to switch between drive modes.

The dash panel, side trims, and other interior elements feature dark ArtVelours microfibre with red topstitching, reinforcing the racetrack-ready interior.

Following the ID. Polo GTI, new ID.3 GTI, and Golf GTI Edition 50, the new ID. Polo Clubsport is the fourth model to debut this year under the performance badge.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000). In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

And American compact car enthusiasts drool over more unobtanium.

The company will showcase the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport concept car at the Essen Motor Show next week, starting on November 27.

Volkswagen didn’t confirm plans to launch a production version, but don’t expect it to reach the States.

The standard VW ID. Polo and GTI are not sold in the US, so the souped-up Clubsport variant likely won’t be either. Hopefully, VW changes its mind and proves us wrong.

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 26, 2026 9:04 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Black Friday 3D printer deals at Amazon and Bambu Lab cover multi-color filament machines, enclosed CoreXY printers, and high-resolution resin models from Creality, Flashforge, Elegoo, and Anycubic. Every link below goes to an individual product page.

If you’re shopping for a first machine, look for automatic bed leveling so you spend weekends printing instead of turning thumbscrews. CoreXY printers move the print head along X and Y while the bed only travels up and down, which keeps prints steady at high speeds. MSLA resin printers cure liquid photopolymer layer by layer with UV light.

Amazon has the Creality K2 Combo at $449, which is $197 under its $645.99 list price. The bundle pairs an enclosed CoreXY printer with a 260 x 260 x 260 mm build volume and one four-spool CFS unit, and Creality rates it for speeds up to 600 mm/s. The 16-color figure in Creality’s marketing takes four CFS units, so plan on four colors per print unless you buy three more.

The Adventurer 5M Pro is the pick here for someone who wants an enclosed printer for ABS or ASA and doesn’t need multi-color. It’s $359 at Amazon, down from a $479 list price. Flashforge lists a 220 x 220 x 220 mm build volume, a 280-degree Celsius quick-swap nozzle, a built-in camera, and a HEPA and carbon filter, and it rates quiet mode at 50 decibels. That build volume is smaller than the 260 mm cube on the K2 Combo above, so check the size of what you plan to print.

Resin is the way to go for miniatures and other small, detailed prints, and the Saturn 4 Ultra 12K is $399.99 at Amazon, a $194 cut from its $593.99 list price. It has a 10-inch 12K monochrome LCD and a tilting vat that peels each cured layer off the release film at an angle. Elegoo rates print speed at up to 150 mm/h. Budget for nitrile gloves, isopropyl alcohol, a wash and cure station, and a ventilated place to work, because resin printing needs all four. Elegoo also sells a 16K version with a sharper screen, so make sure you’re comparing the right model.

The other multi-color machines in this post top out at four colors without add-ons. The Kobra X Combo prints seven out of the box with Anycubic’s ACE 2 Pro filament box, and it’s $449.99 at Amazon (was $569.99). Its build volume is 260 x 260 x 260 mm, and Anycubic says the ACE 2 Pro dries filament at up to 65 degrees Celsius during a print. Reaching the advertised 19 colors takes four ACE 2 Pro units, and Anycubic warns against using cardboard spools in the box.

Bambu Lab’s own sale ends Dec. 1 at 2 a.m. Eastern and includes the dual-nozzle X2D, which succeeds the retired X1-Carbon.

These Amazon deals range from a $169 beginner bed slinger to a four-toolhead machine built to skip purge blocks.

For tabletop miniatures and display figures, MSLA resin printers still beat filament on fine detail.

Damp filament causes stringing and weak layer adhesion, and resin prints need an alcohol wash and UV cure before handling.

#4450. New Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Tips and tools for managing your health and wellbeing during chemo

As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued new guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.

The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.

Under the new guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.

Advances in MRI technology and biomarker testing may also help doctors determine which men need further testing, potentially reducing unnecessary biopsies and overtreatment.

The ACS last updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines in 2010, when conflicting research findings raised questions about whether the benefits of PSA screening outweighed the potential harms.

At the time, the organization emphasized informed, shared decision making between patients and healthcare professionals.

However, longer-term follow-up studies have since provided stronger evidence of the benefits of early detection, prompting the ACS to conduct a systematic review and update its recommendations.

The authors of the report noted, “In making these recommendations, we recognize that PSA testing is only the first step in a screening cascade that includes secondary testing of men with an elevated PSA level and treatment decisions for men diagnosed with prostate cancer.”

The new guidelines recommend a PSA test every 2 years for men ages 50–69 with an average risk of prostate cancer.

The recommendation for those at high risk is a PSA test every year starting at age 45.

For men ages 70–74, the ACS recommends individualized decision making. If an individual chooses to be screened, the ACS recommends a PSA test every 2 years until the age of 74.

Ramkishen Narayanan, MD, Director of the Center for Urologic Health at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline that screening shouldn’t automatically be ruled out for men over 75.

“[A] point worth noting is that for men over 75, their PSA history as well as their individual clinical scenarios should be evaluated, and that PSA should not be discouraged in this group of men if their life expectancy and clinical history warrant a PSA check.”

According to the ACS, approximately 1 in 8 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime.

Individual risk depends on age, race/ethnicity, and other factors:

Prostate cancer diagnoses in the United States increased by around 3% per year between 2014 and 2022, according to the ACS.

The rise in diagnoses, particularly advanced-stage prostate cancer, has renewed attention on the importance of regular screening.

“[The] current state of prostate cancer screening guidelines is vague and generalized. This has led to ambiguity, disagreement, and variation of opinion among healthcare providers and institutions in their approach to men’s health,” said S. Adam Ramin, MD, board certified urologist, urologic oncologist, and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists in Los Angeles, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report.

The updated ACS guidelines drew partly on findings from a 2025 follow-up of the European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC), which found that regular PSA screening was associated with a 13% reduction in prostate cancer deaths over 23 years.

A 12-year ERSPC follow-up in 2012 also suggested that regular screening was associated with a decrease in metastatic prostate cancer diagnosis, which is another finding that influenced the updated guidance.

“Prostate cancer can take many years, even decades, to become clinically significant, so it takes a long time for us to see the consequences of changes in screening practices,” Taylor Goodstein, MD, assistant professor of urology in the College of Medicine at the University of Cincinnati, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline.

“With longer follow-up from randomized trials, we now have more convincing evidence that PSA screening reduces the risk of dying from prostate cancer,” she said.

“The ACS guidelines are important now because they drive home the most important point that prostate cancer screening saves lives,” said Narayanan.

Healthcare professionals use PSA levels to help determine whether additional testing for prostate cancer may be necessary.

The ACS recommends further testing for men under 70 with PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or higher.

For those ages 70 and older, the ACS recommends further testing if their PSA is 6.5 ng/mL or higher. This is because PSA levels tend to be naturally higher in older men.

You can speak with your healthcare professional to find out more about PSA cutoff levels.

Goodstein told Healthline that the ways this new guidance can change the outlook for prostate cancer are simple.

“If we screen men, we can catch troublesome cancers early, before they have a chance to spread,” she said.

Goodstein also emphasized how much the evaluation process has changed. In the past, an elevated PSA level often led directly to a biopsy.

Today, doctors generally repeat the PSA test within two weeks to three months to confirm the result. If PSA levels remain elevated, additional testing, including a prostate MRI or validated biomarker test, can help determine whether a biopsy is necessary.

Narayanan told Healthline, “The new guidelines will hopefully remove any confusion about the value of PSA screening and encourage prostate cancer screening as an integral part of a man’s ‘checkup’.”

He added that it is worth noting that the DRE (digital rectal exam) adds little value to the initial prostate cancer screening and is no longer something that men should fear.

“Adoption of this set of specific guidelines standardizes the approach to screening for prostate cancer. It provides a unified effort among all levels of healthcare. It most likely will increase the chances of finding prostate cancer in earlier stages and lead to improved cancer treatment outcomes,” said Ramin.

#4449. Here’s How the Porsche 718 Boxster EV’s Fake Flat-Six and PDK Work

Porsche chose the 981-generation Boxster GTS model as its sound reference.

The upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend. We just drove a prototype, and while there’s a lot to discuss about the car in general, it’s also worth honing in on the sound aspect. As you might expect, it’s rather pivotal to the experience behind the wheel.

The system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel. Porsche chose the 3.4-liter naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster as its muse. It’s a good choice, but also a bit of a surprise considering the spectacular sound out of the 4.0-liter flat-six found in the previous 718 Boxsters. But Porsche has its reasons, as Dr.-Ing. Sebastian Lefevre, team lead advanced driver assistance systems 718, tells us.

“It was a big discussion in our company,” Lefevre said. “From our point of view, the 4.0 engine is a little bit too soft in the sound. In our company, the 981 GTS sound, six-cylinder, was a little bit louder, and it would also feel more popular and familiar with our old customers.”

Once you hear the sound, there’s a good chance you’ll end up agreeing with Porsche. Lefevre mentioned the possibility of using the four-cylinder from the previous 718, but just as quickly shot the idea down referencing critique of the flat-four’s sound. How it reproduced the engine and exhaust via speakers is similar to how other OEMs with simulated internal combustion engines in EVs do it.

“A lot of microphones outside, inside,” Lefevre said. “And then we measured it all over the complete rpm range. And then we put it here, in this car, and measure it again. With the speakers, which are installed here. We have two.”

The most controversial speaker is bound to be the exterior-positioned one. More than anything, however, this exterior speaker exists as a sound maker for occupants to enjoy when the roof is off. It tries to emulate a mid-engine powertrain arrangement by way of the sound emanating from behind the driver and passenger; Porsche increases the volume inside the car with the roof removed, too. That’s a neat idea, but one that struggles to work in practice; I could hear some faint backfires on “downshifts” like Porsche’s ICE cars produce, but the experience is far from that of a real exhaust and engine echoing and reverberating off mountainsides or buildings.

Mercedes-AMG has the best ICE simulation around right now, with its AMG GT 4-Door Coupe going so far as to induce proper NVH characteristics by using exciters in the seats. The Boxster EV Prototype we drove relies entirely on the speakers to induce its hypnosis. But E-Shift brings a few theatrics to the table.

When lining up for a launch control start, Porsche pulses the torque of the electric motor to give a sense of an impending launch. It also lets you run the car into “redline,” tossing you forward with brake torque, just as it would in a manually-shifted gas-powered car. That said, Porsche took some liberties with the 8000-rpm redline depicted in this prototype; the 981 Boxster GTS instrument cluster shows a redline of 7600 rpm, so you have an extra 400 fake revs to play with in the EV.

Not as though this extra headroom matters, however, as Porsche chose to not simulate the torque curve of the flat-six. Instead, peak performance from the single electric motor is always available, and the car shuffles through its fake seven gears as speeds rise and fall. How it shifts is dependent on drive mode per usual with Porsche PDKs, and you can choose between manual or automatic shifting. You’ll even hear a tone difference in the engine noise over the speakers depending on whether you’re on- or off-throttle, just as you would were the real 3.4-liter be gulping in air behind your head.

For our full first impressions from behind the wheel of the 718 Boxster EV, make sure you read our prototype drive review.

#4447. Tesla FSD approved in Italy, the first big EU market to say yes

Italy’s transport ministry has granted provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” in Europe. Italy becomes the 12th European country to allow the system, and the first of the EU’s big markets.

It also didn’t wait for Brussels. The EU committee that decides on bloc-wide recognition isn’t expected to vote until December at the earliest.

Deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini announced the decision on X on Friday. He wrote that the ministry (MIT) gave the green light after a “thorough technical feasibility check,” and that Italy is getting ahead of the EU recognition process, which he described as “still being defined.”

Tesla Europe followed with a one-liner, “Now approved in Italy, rollout begins soon,” and a video of one of its cars driving itself through Rome. There’s no firm rollout date yet.

It’s still a Level 2 driver-assist system. It can steer, brake, accelerate, and handle intersections and lane changes, but the driver has to supervise at all times and stays fully responsible for the car.

The Dutch vehicle authority RDW was first, approving FSD Supervised on April 10 under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation. Other member states can then recognize that approval nationally, one by one.

Ten did before Italy: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Those are mostly small markets. Together with the Netherlands, they add up to about 70 million people, or roughly 15% of the EU’s population.

Italy alone has about 59 million people, so Friday’s decision nearly doubles the share of Europeans who can legally use the system, to close to 30%.

Rome’s position moved fast. In April, Senator Carlo Calenda formally asked Salvini’s ministry to prioritize the approval. On October 29, Salvini posted that he’d had a “very positive and constructive” call with Elon Musk and that Italy supported a “swift EU approval,” which read at the time as backing for an EU-level decision, not a national one. Three weeks later, Italy went national.

A lot changed in between. Tesla dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe after Germany’s Transport Ministry called it misleading, and cut the maximum speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit. Then on November 16, the RDW approved stricter driver monitoring, including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h. That’s the version Italy is approving.

The EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) pushed the Tesla vote to December after holding only discussions in October. Bloc-wide approval needs a qualified majority: at least 15 of 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Germany said in October it would back approval after Tesla agreed to the rename and the speed cap. If it follows through, Germany and the 12 approving countries would cover roughly 47% of the EU’s population.

That’s progress for Tesla, but it’s not 65%. France refused a national approval in July, and Spain hasn’t recognized the Dutch approval. Tesla needs at least one of them, plus most of the remaining holdouts.

I used FSD for five days this past week. It's impressive on controlled roads.

Even in Chill driving mode, there were still more than a few times that I had to use the Critical feedback.

To think it will ever be perfect is pure fantasy. I will never climb into a automobile that does not have steering controls.

Seven repairs and $10,000 on a leaky roof in two years, with no guarantees. When you factor in Musk, I'm done.

Both Carmax and OnlyUsedTesla acknowledged receiving my requests. No offers from either service 48-hours later. Guess I'm not the only one that's done with Tesla.

This is a real win for Tesla, and for Italian owners with HW4 cars who have been paying for a feature they couldn’t use at home. Italy is Tesla’s first big European market to say yes, and it shifts momentum going into December.

But it’s pretty crazy that now Europe is going to get a safer FSD than in the US.

I bet that this will get reflected in the data, if we ever get to see it.

#4444. Robert Wickens Will Run a Full IMSA Season In a BMW M4 GT3

Wickens will make his 24 Hours of Daytona debut this upcoming January.

Eight years after a harrowing crash at Pocono Raceway paralyzed the then-IndyCar star, Robert Wickens has made his way to the grid of the biggest sports car race in the United States. He will contest the 2027 installment of the 24 Hours of Daytona in a Hanley Motorsports Inc.-run BMW M4 GT3, part of his first-ever full season of IMSA racing.

Wickens will pair with Mason Filippi in a full-season effort in the GTD class. Both drivers are champions in the IMSA Pilot Challenge TCR class; Wickens won the title in 2023, while Filippi scored his own championship in 2026. The pairing reunites two drivers that shared a DXDT Racing Corvette during the sprint races last season, the second such schedule for Wickens in the past two years. Their 2026 season was briefly interrupted when the team’s hauler caught fire on its way to the round at Laguna Seca.

Since those were all sprint races, Wickens would only have to get into or out of the car one time per race event. Endurance races are a new challenge, one that will mean more driver changes complicated by his paralysis. It will also mean more chances to win, and opportunities to win his class in the country’s oldest and most prestigious sports car events. That opportunity is an exciting one, the biggest step yet what Wickens hopes is a long road back to the top.

“I’ve worked incredibly hard for a long time to reach this point in my career,” Wickens says, “and I’m filled with gratitude for everyone who has helped me achieve my goal of returning to the highest levels of motorsports... I couldn’t be more excited to get to work and compete in my first full season in the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship.”

#4443. Mind Games: My ‘Secret’ to Enjoying Coffee Without Anxiety

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A guide to therapy, medications, and techniques for managing anxiety

Nutrition tips and tools for supporting mental well-being

Resources for finding and receiving therapy

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and lessons learned about what it means to be mentally well.

Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.

My morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m. if I drink it past noon. As an already anxious human, the last thing I need is to exacerbate my symptoms, even if it’s coming from a delicious source.

Over a year ago, I noticed that my anxiety was higher than usual. I was also tossing and turning and waking up at all hours of the night for weeks on end.

One night in particular, I woke up every hour for 8 hours. Naturally, I wanted to blame it on the full moon or anything other than my beloved coffee, but alas, I realized that my caffeine consumption was the most likely culprit.

Could I have aimed to set a strict drinking schedule to see if that fixed things? Sure. But instead, I decided to quit cold turkey and undergo an experiment to see how I’d feel going coffee-free for the first time in years.

Over the next 8 months, I’d swap my coffee station for a matcha setup, dabble in exotic herbal blends from my local teahouse, and become a self-proclaimed tea connoisseur. Lo and behold, my anxiety eased up, and my sleep quality improved, too.

Fast forward to 4 months ago, when I hopped back on the coffee train. But this time, I’m relying on a handy amino acid to help avoid anxiety and other unwanted side effects: L-theanine.

Health and wellness touch everyone’s life differently. This is one person’s story. The views and opinions expressed are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Healthline Media and should not serve as a substitute for medical advice from a healthcare professional.

L-theanine is mainly found in green and black tea and one type of wild mushroom. The mental health benefits of L-theanine consumption are an emerging area of research, but one 2024 review found that consuming around 200 to 400 milligrams (mg) may help relieve symptoms in people with anxiety disorders.

Still, anecdotal reports suggest there may be benefits of adding L-theanine to coffee. Over the last 5 years, the combo has been gaining traction on Reddit and TikTok for managing caffeine-related side effects.

Despite an overwhelming amount of rave reviews online, I couldn’t find much research to support these claims, so I spoke with a neurologist to see if they had any thoughts.

“This trend has real science behind it,” said Fawad Mian, MD, who is board certified in neurology, clinical neurophysiology, and sleep medicine and the founder of Ascend Regenerative.

“Controlled studies show caffeine plus L-theanine improves focus and attention more than caffeine alone, and some suggest it softens caffeine’s side effects, like tiredness, headaches, and blood pressure spikes,” Mian said. “It smooths caffeine’s effects but doesn’t erase them, so it’s not a license to drink more coffee,” he added.

With all of this in mind, especially after realizing just how calm I was while drinking black and green teas during my coffee break, I decided to give it a try.

After about 4 months of “testing,” I’ve found that adding L-theanine to my coffee works extremely well for me.

No more anxiety, scatterbrain, shakiness, or staying up until 3 a.m. And no lifestyle overhaul needed. The supplement, which I prefer in liquid form, has become a seamless addition to my daily routine.

Every morning, I make a fresh batch of French press coffee with (strong) local beans, then I squeeze some L-theanine into my cup.

I’ve noticed that I get the usual coffee benefits like improved focus and concentration, plus a nice, calm, stable energy throughout the day.

Even if I drink it until 2 p.m., I’m fighting to keep my eyes open at night before I finally fall asleep around 10. Perhaps this is because L-theanine may also support quality sleep.

Mindful L-Theanine Drops is the liquid supplement that I use every day.

I add a one-second squeeze (which contains 200 mg of L-theanine) into my morning coffee, then I’m good to go. I even started carrying a bottle in my bag just in case I get a latte from a coffee shop on a whim.

You can also add it to a glass of water, a cup of tea, or another drink of your choosing. It’s unflavored, so it doesn’t alter the taste of your drinks. Real secret stuff.

Out of curiosity, and because I’m a natural skeptic and overthinker, I asked Mian if my positive experience could be a placebo effect, or if I’m seeing real results.

“Expectation may play a small role, but the effect is biologically plausible,” he said. “L-theanine boosts calming brain activity that offsets caffeine’s stimulation, and 200 mg matches the doses used in studies.” However, he noted that it doesn’t speed caffeine clearance, so drinking coffee only in the morning still matters for sleep quality.

While L-theanine is generally safe to consume, it’s best to speak with a healthcare professional first, especially if you’re pregnant, nursing, receiving cancer treatment, or taking blood pressure medication or sedatives.

“Choose a third-party tested brand, and if caffeine makes you anxious, cutting back is still the simplest fix,” Mian added.

So, if you’re anything like me and drinking coffee also leads to anxiety and jitters for you, I highly recommend trying this supplement once you get the green light from your doctor. It’s been working for me. It may work well for you, too.

💌 Over to you: I’d love to hear your thoughts on this. Does coffee also give you unwanted side effects? Have you tried L-theanine to remedy them? Let me know, or ask any questions about my experience by emailing me here.

#4442. Renault undercuts BYD with a new EV that costs less than $20,000

The new Renault Twingo E-Tech is among the most affordable vehicles, electric or gas-powered, starting at just £14,745 in the UK, or under $20,000.

Another affordable, practical EV the US will never see. Renault’s new Twingo E-Tech is an electric remake of its iconic 1990s city car.

The retro-looking EV went on sale in Europe earlier this year, starting at under €20,000 ($22,000), before government incentives. In places like Germany, it starts at about €13,990 ($15,500), including the €6,000 ($6,600) federal EV grant.

In the UK, Renault announced that prices for the Twingo E-Tech will start at just £14,745, or about $19,500. That includes the government’s Electric Clean Car Grant (ECG) of £3,750 ($4,900).

At that price, Renault’s new electric car is among the most affordable vehicles available, including gas-powered cars.

It’s cheaper than the gas-powered Dacia Sandero (£14,765) and BYD’s cheapest EV, the Dolphin Surf (£18,675). Only a few cars are lower-priced, including the Dacia Spring (£11,990) and Leapmotor T03 (£12,995).

What do you get for the price? At just 3,790 mm (149.2″) long, the electric city car is a bit smaller than the Hyundai Inster and the BYD Dolphin Surf.

For those in the US, that’s even smaller than the first-generation Chevy Bolt EV, which measured 4,145 mm (163.2″) in length.

Despite its compact size, the “cheeky, practical” 5-door city car, as Renault calls it, offers up to 360 liters of boot capacity. It also features independent, sliding 50/50 folding rear seats to haul bigger items like a surfboard.

With up to 50 kW DC fast charging, Renault said the Twingo E-Tech can charge from 15% to 80% in 28 minutes.

The base Renault Twingo E-Tech Evolution, priced from £14,745 ($19,500), uses a 27.5 kWh LFP battery and an 80 hp (60 kW) motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range.

The entry-level version features 16″ steel wheels, a 7″ driver display, 10″ navigation screen, and ADAS features, including cruise control and lane-keep assist.

Renault will offer three Twingo E-Tech trims in total. The mid-range Techno trim gains 18″ wheels, Google built-in with Renault’s Reno avatar, a reversing camera, automatic climate control, a hands-free key card, One Pedal driving, and heated front seats. It starts at £16,245 ($21,500), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG.

With Google built in, drivers can easily find and navigate to charging stations via Google Maps, use Google Gemini AI virtual assistance, or access over 100 apps, including Waze and Amazon Music.

At least this car has some styling unlike the generic box style VW offerings in this category. In this size car I prefer the SUV style of the Dacia Spring for myself, but of course we will never see any of these wonderful cars in the USA.

The top-spec Twingo E-Tech Launch Edition, priced from £17,645 ($23,200), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG, adds a suite of ADAS features, including blind-spot warning, rear cross-traffic alert and hands-free parking.

Inside, the Launch Edition features a special mottled textile upholstery with red stitching and premium floor mats.

Renault is offering a special promo for those who buy a new Twingo E-Tech through Mobilize Financial Services on a PCP or HP agreement by June 30, 2027, which includes two years’ free servicing.

Interested buyers can purchase the Twingo R Pass for £100, giving them priority access to ordering, a mini Twingo E-Tech model, and a green Renault key cover.

#4439. New York Just Made It Harder for Automakers to Put Car Features Behind a Paywall

A new law takes aim at subscription fees for features already built into your vehicle, but automakers can still charge for certain services.

These days, the average new car payment in America is over $800 a month. With a payment like that, the last thing you want is to pay even more to access all of your car’s features. The state of New York is now taking steps to ensure that won’t happen; however, like most things in life, there are exceptions.

On Monday, November 23, New York governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation restricting automakers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees to access certain features already installed in their vehicles. Essentially, if the hardware necessary to operate a feature is already installed in the vehicle, and activating that feature doesn't require continued support or expense on the part of the automaker, dealer, or third-party service provider, it cannot be put behind a subscription paywall.

A few years ago, BMW faced backlash in Europe for charging a monthly fee in order to enjoy heated seats. BMW has since backed away from that plan, and under this new legislation, that subscription approach would no longer be legal. According to a report by the New York Post, companies that violate this new law will face a $250 fine per subscription.

However, this doesn’t mean that New Yorkers can wave goodbye to all automotive-related subscription services; automakers can still charge for navigation updates, satellite radio, infotainment services, in-car Wi-Fi, roadside assistance, and certain connected vehicle services. Also, software-dependent driver-assistance and automated driving features like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving and General Motors’s Super Cruise are also exempt, meaning motorists shouldn't expect their hands-free highway driving subscriptions to suddenly become cost-free too.

Automakers and third-party companies have about 90 days to get into compliance before the law takes effect on February 27, 2027. It will be interesting to see if other states will follow New York’s lead, but the bigger question is if automakers will simply begin charging more for optional equipment at the time of purchase.

#4436. Targeted conversion of carbon dioxide into chemical feedstocks: CO₂ helps shape its own catalyst

Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. #4435. How to Plan Your Holiday Meals in a Year of Unprecedented Recalls

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Following a series of high-profile food recalls and outbreaks this year, many Americans may be concerned about keeping their families safe from foodborne illness during the holidays.

In fact, according to a recent national survey by Orlando Health, around 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years.

Although several major foodborne illness outbreaks have ended and their associated recalls are no longer active, food safety remains an important concern. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 48 million people in the United States experience foodborne illness each year.

However, there are simple steps you can take to reduce the risk of foodborne illness when preparing holiday meals and storing leftovers.

While there were several food recalls in the United States over the summer, two of the largest involved Salmonella linked to jalapeños and Cyclospora linked to lettuce.

These outbreaks prompted widespread recalls and raised concerns about the safety of certain foods, particularly fresh produce.

Although health officials have since declared the major outbreaks over, some consumers may still be hesitant to purchase foods associated with previous recalls.

Even with this declaration, you may still feel nervous about purchasing certain foods, but experts say you don’t need to worry.

“Here in the United States, we have the safest food supply in the world. The recent recalls show that our food safety system is working,” said William Schaffner, MD, Professor, Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University.

Michelle Routhenstein, preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, told Healthline that past recalls do not mean entire food categories need to be avoided. The important thing is whether the specific product you have matches a current recall, based on details such as brand, lot number, package size, and expiration date.

“You should enjoy familiar foods, including properly cooked poultry, washed fruits and vegetables, and pasteurized dairy products,” she said. “The key is checking relevant recalls and practicing safe food handling.”

“Before shopping or cooking, review FDA and USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) recall information and compare any relevant notices with the labels on your ingredients,” said Routhenstein.

Check the pantry and freezer, too: something purchased months ago may still be affected.

“Stay alert to any news reports about food recalls and use good food preparation practices. Those simple actions should keep your holidays happy and safe,” said Schaffner.

Consumers can sign up for food recall alerts through the FDA or visit FoodSafety.gov for recall information from both the FDA and USDA.

Schaffner emphasized the importance of following safe food-handling practices when preparing everyday meals and holiday gatherings.

“Remember the longstanding advice: keep food hot or cold. Avoid long times at room temperature,” he said.

Routhenstein advised focusing on four basics: clean, separate, cook, and chill.

Schaffner noted the importance of refrigerating leftovers promptly rather than leaving them at room temperature for extended periods. He recommends clearing the table and refrigerating leftovers soon after the meal ends.

Routhenstein reiterated that you should refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours rather than leaving them out to cool.

Divide turkey into smaller portions and transfer sides and gravy into shallow containers to help them cool quickly, she advised.

Leftovers can typically be stored in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. If you don’t plan to eat them within that time, consider freezing them.

The important thing is to keep an eye out for any new recalls, practice food safety, and enjoy your holiday meals!

#4434. Stellantis Is Ending Factory WEC Racing, While Promising More Performance Cars

Stellantis is also withdrawing from Formula E as part of efforts to redirect racing expertise toward the likes of Alfa Romeo and Maserati.

Alfa Romeo and Maserati each have plenty of history they can leverage. Getting American buyers excited to snap up what's current or excited about what’s next has proven much harder, though. Now, a retreat by Stellantis from motorsport could give both brands the engineering attention they need.

On November 23, Stellantis announced that it was ending its participation in the World Endurance Championship at the end of this year; next year, it'll end its efforts in Formula E once the season is over. Its new priorities are customer racing and high-performance vehicle development. Alfa Romeo and Maserati are explicitly named as beneficiaries of that expertise.

Perhaps most notably, Stellantis intends to retain and redeploy affected employees, including into performance-car development. That could put people accustomed to solving problems at the highest end of motorsport into roles where they help customers enjoy their cars on public roads.

There's certainly plenty for these brands to do on that front. Alfa Romeo sold just 2316 vehicles in the United States through September, down 52 percent from the same period last year. Its third-quarter total was 569 cars across the Giulia, Stelvio, and Tonale. Whatever affection Americans might have for the badge, it isn’t translating into much showroom traffic.

Maserati, meanwhile, has fresh material to work with; its updated North American lineup includes a 385-hp Grecale V-6, and 582-hp Trofeo versions of the GranTurismo and GranCabrio. Those are solid offerings, but when it comes to marketing, there's plenty of room for the brand to grow.

Of course, there’s a sizable financial caveat: Stellantis hasn’t disclosed expected savings from the withdrawals or promised an accompanying increase in, for example, American marketing spending. It reported a €453 million ($497 million) net loss and negative industrial free cash flow of roughly €4 billion ($4.4 billion) in the third quarter. Any freed-up cash will have plenty of competing demands. That said, it's great to see that Stellantis directly emphasizing that the end of the WEC and Formula E programs will mean more resources go to Alfa and Maserati production cars—and “high-performance models” at that.

Each Nova unit delivers 500 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of energy and 200 kilowatts (kW) of power. It has a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.7 x 5.9 ft) footprint, and units can be linked together for projects in the tens of megawatt-hours. A site could charge the batteries when electricity is cheaper or when its solar panels are producing more than it needs, then draw on that power when demand spikes or the grid goes down.

Nova can use packs from different EV models, even when those packs have aged at different rates. Moment’s battery management software tracks how each pack is doing. As packs wear out, the company can replace them while leaving the enclosure and concrete pad in place. Moment says its pack replacement service could keep a system in service for more than 20 years.

“We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chains. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering, and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid,” said Edward Chiang, co-founder and CEO of Moment Energy.

Moment Energy says Nova is the first storage system built from retired EV batteries to earn both UL 1973 certification for the batteries and UL 9540 certification for the complete system. It was also tested under UL 9540A, which looks at how a battery fire can spread. The factory itself is certified under UL 1974, which covers how used batteries are assessed and graded for reuse.

That matters for businesses with limited space. Nova is designed to sit outdoors alongside the buildings it serves. It uses liquid cooling, detects smoke, heat, and flammable gases, and is rated to operate from −13F to 122F (−25C to 50C).

Moment Energy also says an independent review found that Nova meets US federal sourcing restrictions tied to the clean electricity investment tax credit. Those rules are one part of determining whether a project qualifies for the credit.

Orders are open, and Moment Energy expects the first units to ship in Q1 2027 for deployments across North America.

#4429. The Improbable Success of a ‘Poky Little Motoring Show’

Top Gear’s worldwide fame was a happy accident.

Through the lens of time, the early part of the Aughts can seem like a simpler age when phones were usually dumb, politicians were sometimes smart, and families gathered quaintly around one TV set to watch the same program at the same time. High-resolution internet video and the streaming revolution were distant spots on the horizon. But the changing landscape unwittingly created the perfect conditions for an accidental phenomenon: a TV show about cars with an estimated global audience of 350 million, a broadcasting triumph that would be impossible to replicate today. Because the Aughts was the decade that seeded the improbable success of a self-confessed “poky little motoring show” called Top Gear.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

In fact, Top Gear predated this century, debuting on BBC television in 1977 and plodding through the Eighties and Nineties with sensible car-buying advice and cozy trips to steam rallies. The series added Jeremy Clarkson to its hosting lineup in 1988 to bring a bit of wit to what was still a fundamentally earnest format. In 1999, he left the show, and two years later, the BBC announced that Top Gear was going to be “rested,” a polite British way of saying “canceled.”

At the same time, Jeremy and an old school friend, TV producer Andy Wilman, who had been a lesser Top Gear presenter, were working on plans for a bigger, more boisterous car show called Carmageddon. When the pair pitched it to the head of the BBC Two channel, she liked the idea and agreed to commission the show with one proviso: Carmageddon should become a reboot of Top Gear. The fuse had been lit, but free­wheeling global success wasn’t the master plan. In fact, there was no grand scheme, only a vague hope to make a halfway-­decent show for audiences in the U.K. I know this because from 2002 to 2015, I was Top Gear’s script editor.

This, like so much of the show, was something of an accident. I’d worked briefly with Jeremy on the old version of Top Gear, and he’d liked my satirical car website, Sniff Petrol, but if I hadn’t bumped into him in a restaurant and been invited to “come in for a chat,” perhaps the opportunity would have passed me by. As it is, I went to see Jeremy and Andy, and I listened to their ideas, many of which sounded strange. A racing driver who couldn’t tell you anything about a car because he never spoke? A segment forcing celebrities to drive around a track in a low-budget grocery getter? An indoor studio for a car show? Hmm. But Jeremy and Andy are persuasive people, and I agreed to join nonetheless.

We auditioned a lot of people to co-host and eventually found Richard Hammond, a car journalist who performed an unremarkable screen test but then reduced us to hysterics with self-deprecating stories as he was walking toward the exit.

We made a pilot episode, which was a disaster, then a second pilot episode, which was also a disaster, after which point there was no time to try again because we had a scheduled on-air date. We’d go to the pub after work and sit there making despairing sighs and ask, “What are we doing?” We were not plotting world domination. Our biggest goal was to get a show out on time so the BBC didn’t have to broadcast reruns instead.

But we were allowed to carry on, and our first season attracted modest viewing figures, just passing the low target the BBC had issued. Back then, some broadcasters were willing to nurture shows and let them grow gently rather than demanding instant success.

Top Gear needed this patience because it often felt like we were making it up as we went along. In the popular consciousness, the show is remembered for Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, and James May driving malfunctioning cars across harsh and distant lands. But it didn’t start like that at all. We didn’t have James in season one (BBC management thought he was too similar to Jeremy); instead, a car dealer called Jason Dawe was in the third spot. We didn’t go abroad because we were a British show and thought we should film in the U.K., no matter how gray and rainy it might be. We didn’t put the three hosts together in the field until the fourth season, an experiment that yielded nuggets of gold. We never planned to create epic road trips occupying entire shows, until a journey across the Southern United States generated too much material to squeeze into a 20-minute film and was allowed to roam free as an hour-long special.

What we did have from the start was a certain editorial rigor. Jeremy began his career as a local newspaper journalist. Richard had a background in live radio. James worked on car magazines for years. They’d grown up in worlds that demanded quick thinking and an endless supply of ideas. Sometimes Jeremy would stride into the office booming, “I’ve had a thought . . . .” Sometimes we’d sit around, batting stupid notions back and forth.

As part of my job, I’d scribble down what we said, then try to hack the best bits into something workable. After that came the important part. Any idea, no matter how brilliant it first seemed, was then poked and prodded and dismantled to make sure it was as good as it could be. When we had a full episode’s worth of vetted ideas, I’d sit down with one or all of the presenters, and we’d write a script. For a solo track test, this would be detailed and extensive. For a three-header out in the field, the introduction would be tightly written to make sure our mission was clear, in our minds and to the viewers, after which there would be rough scene headings and perhaps the odd one-liner. As a production team, we’d plan situations and challenges that we thought would allow the hosts to run free with ad-libs and arguing.

Jeremy, Richard, and James were very different people with a love of cars as their common ground. We never had to fake their on-screen personalities; that’s just who they were. Jeremy, bombastic and attention seeking. Richard, excitable and a verbal sniper with killer one-­liners. James, often giving the impression that he’d rather be at home dis­mantling a motorcycle than forced to hang out with these two morons. The dynamic worked.

That such a poorly planned piece of programming eventually found itself a global success is down to the decade in which it was born, a time when people still watched the same show at the same time. One inadvertent stroke of genius was the BBC’s decision to schedule Top Gear on a Sunday evening, traditionally a quiet night on TV in the U.K. Among straight-faced detective shows and florid costume dramas, the hijinks of Top Gear—a nun in a monster truck, a bus jumping motorcycles, a man trying to destroy a To­yota Hilux in increasingly elaborate ways—shone like a beacon of eccentricity. The next morning, everyone could go into work or school and talk about it.

Ratings grew steadily. Then, during filming in 2006 for the ninth season, Richard crashed a jet-­propelled dragster. The show was paused while he recovered from serious injuries. When we returned, viewing figures in the U.K. jumped dramatically.

Global success came later, especially with the growth of YouTube and other social media. ­Suddenly anyone could clip out their favorite bits of Top Gear and make them accessible all around the world. An American gearhead called Alex Mills founded a site called FinalGear, where fans could discuss Top Gear and share BitTorrent links so people everywhere could download the show, if not entirely legally. Top Gear became cult viewing in countries where car shows weren’t trying to turn pickup trucks into boats and a three-wheeled car into a space shuttle. Which was, of course, everywhere else.

Also, the car landscape of the Aughts gave the show great material upon which to build. It was the era of the hypercar, and at its peak was that stats-heavy poster child, the Bugatti Veyron. But it was also a time when Subaru and Mitsubishi were slugging it out to make the best roadgoing rally car. Countless manufacturers were serving up everything from high-powered wagons to hyperactive hot hatches. Best of all, in the U.K. at least, secondhand cars were fantastically cheap and accessible, even old supercars.

At the time, living hand to mouth simply trying to get the show done, we didn’t realize how lucky we were, though I hope we made the most of the luck that came our way. The reports of ever-­bigger audiences seemed abstract and unbelievable. Only when it became harder and harder to find any country in the world where our filming presence wouldn’t attract a large and excitable crowd did we start to realize that perhaps this stupid show of ours was catching on.

Nonetheless, we rarely had time to rest on our laurels. Indeed, Andy Wilman actively tried to stop us from becoming full of ourselves by, among other things, stridently discouraging attempts to make our disgustingly shabby offices nicer. He believed we had a job to do, and that job was to make an hour of entertainment for Sunday nights on BBC television. The rest was an implausible-­sounding bonus. And perhaps by dint of not trying too hard to be globally appealing, Top Gear became a worldwide phenomenon of the Aughts and beyond. It really couldn’t have happened at any other time.

#4427. Planning to Stop Taking a GLP-1? Here’s How to Maintain Weight Loss

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Switching GLP-1 medications or undergoing bariatric surgery may help people maintain greater weight loss than stopping treatment entirely, according to a new study presented at ObesityWeek and published in eClinicalMedicine on November 14.

The Cleveland Clinic study compared five strategies for managing weight after treatment with GLP-1 medications, analyzing data from 20,486 adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes.

People who stop taking GLP-1 medications often regain weight. Researchers examined whether continuing treatment, switching medications, or undergoing bariatric surgery could help limit weight regain or support further weight loss.

The findings showed that people who underwent bariatric surgery or switched between semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) experienced the greatest overall weight loss.

The study participants had an average age of 56.7 years, an average weight of 109 kg (240.3 lbs), and an average body mass index (BMI) of 38. All had been taking either semaglutide or tirzepatide for at least 90 days.

The researchers categorized the participants into five groups:

After 2 years, those who underwent bariatric surgery saw an average loss of 28.2% of their body weight or about 31.5 kg (69.4 lbs).

“We increasingly view medications and surgery as complementary tools rather than competing ones,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“For patients with severe obesity (typically a BMI of 35 or higher, or 30+ with metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes), bariatric surgery remains the most durable, cost-effective intervention available,” he added. “Using a GLP-1 beforehand can safely reduce liver volume and lower surgical risk, while surgery provides the permanent anatomical and hormonal reset needed to maintain that weight loss long-term without relying indefinitely on weekly injections.”

During the same period, those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide lost 16% of their body weight, or about 18 kg (39.6 lbs).

Participants who switched from semaglutide to tirzepatide lost 3 kg (6.6 lbs) more than those who continued taking semaglutide. However, participants already taking tirzepatide lost 4.5 kg (9.9 lbs) more by continuing treatment rather than switching to semaglutide.

The other groups experienced lower amounts of weight loss:

After one year, participants with type 2 diabetes experienced HbA1c reductions of 1.76% following bariatric surgery, 1.43% after switching GLP-1 medications, and 1.32% after continuing their original medication, compared with 0.48% among those who discontinued treatment entirely.

After one year, participants with hypertension (high blood pressure) also experienced greater reductions in blood pressure following surgery or switching GLP-1 medications than those who discontinued treatment entirely.

“[This study] reinforces the need for a long term, multi-modal continuum of care rather than treating GLP-1s as a temporary fix,” said Ali.

Ali also recommended the following strategies to help maintain weight loss after stopping a GLP-1 medication:

The findings highlight the importance of having a long-term weight management plan in place before stopping a GLP-1 medication.

Before stopping a GLP-1 medication, talk with a healthcare professional. They can help you explore your options and determine which strategies may be most appropriate for your health needs.

Ali told Healthline that identifying the reason for stopping treatment is an important first step. He noted that people often discontinue GLP-1 medications because of gastrointestinal side effects, supply issues, or loss of insurance coverage rather than because they no longer need treatment.

He said that if side effects are the issue, adjusting the dose or switching to a different agent often solves the problem.

Ali also emphasized that stopping a GLP-1 medication shouldn’t be viewed as a test of willpower. Increased hunger after discontinuing treatment is a biological response, not a personal failure.

“Have a concrete ‘off-ramp’ plan in place with your doctor before taking your last dose, so you have medical, nutritional, or surgical support ready to protect the health gains you worked hard to achieve,” advised Ali.

#4426. BYD offers a first look at its new flagship people mover

BYD is preparing to launch a new flagship MPV soon after previewing the large people mover for the first time.

We knew it was coming soon after images of the camouflaged multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) began flooding the internet last month.

Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, confirmed the new flagship MPV is coming soon.

“A new creation for the times, born for the family,” Zhuo said after posting a preview of it for the first time on his Weibo account on Friday.

The new flagship Ocean MPV is “coming soon,” according to Zhuo, but he didn’t reveal a specific debut date. He previously said the company expects to launch its first MPV under the Ocean lineup by the end of 2026, so local reports suggest it will make an official debut next week at the 2026 Guangzhou Auto show, which kicks off on November 27.

Although it’s blurred, the preview shows a similar shape and size to the recent spy images, with a roof-mounted LiDAR and traditional pull-style door handles.

It doesn’t appear to look much like the futuristic Ocean-V concept BYD unveiled at the 2026 Beijing Auto Show earlier this year, a preview of its first MPV under the Ocean series.

The concept featured a sliding center display screen and two different modes: Camping and Movie. In camping mode, the seats either fold flat to create a bed or swivel to face each other.

In Movie mode, the vehicle transforms into a private mobile theater with a large display screen that flips out of the dashboard.

While it may not have some of the more extravagant elements from the concept, the Ocean MPV is expected to be “flagship-worthy,” if you will, with BYD’s latest tech and other premium features like zero-gravity seats and plenty of digital screens.

The Ocean-V’s innovations “will gradually make their way into mass-production vehicles,” BYD said earlier this year.

BYD has yet to announce any details, but the flagship Ocean MPV is expected to be about the size of the Xia, a large plug-in hybrid minivan sold under its Dynasty lineup.

The BYD Xia measures 5,145 mm long, 1,970 mm wide, and 1,805 mm tall, with a 3,045 mm wheelbase.

Like the Xia, the Ocean MPV is expected to use BYD’s latest-generation DM-i plug-in hybrid system with a 1.5L engine and a 200 kW electric motor.

The Xia starts at 249,800 yuan ($37,500) in China. It’s available with two BYD Blade LFP battery packs: 20.4 kWh and 36.6 kWh, providing pure electric CLTC ranges of 100 km (62 miles) and 218 km (135 miles). On a full tank of gas and full charge, the plug-in people mover offers a combined CLTC range of 1,163 km (722 miles).

BYD also sells the flagship Denza D9 MPV under its luxury sub-brand. With the Denza D9 starting above 300,000 yuan and the Xia at around 250,000 yuan, the Ocean MPV is expected to fill the gap.

Zhuo said to stay tuned for more coming soon, so check back for updates.

#4423. Elon Musk freezes at awkward Tesla Argentina launch: ‘I don’t know what to say’

Tesla officially launched in Argentina on Friday with President Javier Milei on stage in Buenos Aires, and Elon Musk joined by video from his plane to welcome the brand’s newest market. It didn’t go well.

Musk got through one line about Tesla before stalling out: “Sorry, I don’t really know what I want to say.” The call ended about two minutes in, without any real pitch for the Model 3 or Model Y that Tesla had just put on sale.

The launch took place at Arenas Studio in Buenos Aires’ La Boca neighborhood. Milei spoke for less than eight minutes, then the host asked the room to welcome “our next guest,” and Musk popped up on the giant screen from what looked like an airplane cabin. Milei burst out laughing and bounced on his feet.

Musk started fine: “Hello, Argentina. Well, here we are. It’s a joy to share Tesla with all of you and to establish ourselves there.”

JAJAJAJ QUE ES ESTO, Milei lo llamó de sorpresa a Elon Musk para que diga algo sobre el local de Tesla inaugurado y es lo mas INCÓMODO que vas a ver en tu vida, se quería ir a la mierda y COLGÓ, durísimo, ni Elon Musk lo soporta al gordo pelotudo pic.twitter.com/CrJkv4iu1x

Then he started glancing off to each side. “Actually, I don’t really know what to say, other than thank you for this welcome to Tesla in Argentina,” he said. He briefly mentioned a charging network with state-owned oil company YPF, thanked the audience again, and then: “Sorry, I don’t really know what I want to say.”

And that was it. The feed cut before he even said goodbye.

Milei tried to save it. Back on stage, he told the crowd that “those who do a lot, talk little,” and called Musk “the Leonardo da Vinci of the 21st century.”

The clip is now spreading fast in Argentina, with one post of the video racking up over 1.1 million views overnight.

Tesla opened online orders on Friday for five versions of the Model 3 and Model Y, all imported from Gigafactory Shanghai. Here are the list prices, VAT included:

Tesla adds about $600 in reservation, destination, and documentation fees on top of that, and first deliveries aren’t expected until March or April 2027. There are no dealers. Sales happen online, with showroom space at the Unicenter and Alcorta Shopping malls in Buenos Aires.

Argentina is Tesla’s fourth direct-sales market in South America after Chile, Colombia, and Uruguay, which launched in July. Tesla is late to the party, though. BYD already leads Argentina’s EV market after Milei’s government cut import taxes on electric vehicles.

What I really found awkward was hearing Musk stating "I'm not MAGA, I'm not sure what MAGA means" in his interview with CNBC.

Especially surprising after he declared, "I’m not just MAGA; I’m 'Dark MAGA,'" after spending half a billion dollars to support MAGA candidates, and after promoting the MAGA political agenda (which he has, in part, personally implemented through the DOGE).

At this point, I expect him to reappear in the guise of a Democrat and write a big, fat, one-billion-dollar check to a Democratic super PAC for the 2028 election cycle.

I am sure Musk has a lot on his mind right now, but selling Tesla vehicles clearly isn’t one of them, because he couldn’t come up with anything to say about it.

Launching a new market has one job: get people excited to buy the cars. Musk had a sitting president cheering for him on stage, a room full of fans, and every camera in Buenos Aires pointed at him. He couldn’t come up with a single reason to buy a Model Y.

This isn’t stage fright. Musk has been telling investors for two years that Tesla’s future is robotaxis and Optimus robots, not selling cars. Meanwhile, Tesla’s deliveries fell 8.6% to 1.636 million in 2025, its second annual decline in a row. The guy who is behind the brand doesn’t care about selling these cars anymore, and this clip shows it better than anything I’ve seen.

#4421. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Why One Big Meal Isn’t the Real Holiday Health Problem

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In the classic Thanksgiving comedy Planes, Trains and Automobiles, hapless hero Del Griffith (played by the late, great John Candy) delivers an emotional riposte to Steve Martin’s uptight ad man Neal Page that stands as a beautifully dignified defense of kindness, empathy and self-love in the face of his own perceived shortcomings.

“You want to hurt me? Go right ahead if it makes you feel any better…I could be a cold, hard cynic like you. But I don’t like to hurt people’s feelings. You think what you want about me, I’m not changing. I… I like me. My wife likes me…because I’m the real article. What you see is what you get.”

For many of us around the holidays, particularly after a night of excess, Del and Neal’s exchange could read as our internal monologue – your kinder inner voice battling the internal bully who judges your every overindulgence. The jury’s out on whether the kind voice is ever as potent as Del’s is in that moment. But it should be, because when it comes to your health around the holidays, the bully has usually got it wrong.

The truth is, for most of us, one day of immoderation during Thanksgiving is unlikely to matter in the grand scheme. As such, you would do well to avoid the litany of holiday season health myths out there, many of which seem hell-bent on punishing you for taking a day off:

Like all misinformation, these kinds of medical myths are loud and tend to die hard, but they almost always trade on quick fixes that target the wrong thing.

A 2020 review of 23 observational studies found that most showed significant weight gain during festive periods, averaging roughly a pound and a half. One of the original studies, a landmark NIH study from 2000, found that much of that weight tends to stick around. So the question is not what you ate on Thanksgiving Thursday and how quickly you can “undo the damage,” but rather whether the extended holiday season becomes a two-month period where your healthy routine goes out the window. Some things to look out for on that front:

None of this is a free pass for everyone. If you manage a health condition, you likely have less margin for error, even when talking about a single meal or a drink. Critical factors include timing, sodium intake, alcohol intake, and missed medication. A few non-exhaustive examples:

Whatever condition you’re managing, the move for all of them remains the same – be prepared. Check your plan with your care team before the holiday, not after, and call them if something feels off afterward.

Technically, feeling good on Black Friday starts on Thursday. A short and light walk after a feast can help smooth out post-meal blood sugar – the earlier the better, ideally within an hour of eating. Staying upright for a couple of hours to help with digestion, particularly if you’re prone to reflux, is also a great idea. If you’re on medication, remember to take it on time. And, at the risk of sounding prudish, and this goes for everyone: try to get to bed at a sensible hour.

Above all else, Thanksgiving is a holiday built around gratitude and kindness, so channel your inner Del Griffith and remember to be both grateful and kind, to yourself and to those around you – evidence suggests that’s also good for your health.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.
